If we want to move beyond general statements and identify the different positions taken by modern Arab researchers toward our intellectual heritage, we need to return briefly to the earlier classification we used for the main ways of studying it. These modern positions have not completely broken with those older approaches.
Let us recall them briefly, so that we can build directly on them without treating the list as exhaustive:
An approach that treats the history of thought as a history of individual thinkers and their personal ideas.
A mechanical approach to the exchange between different cultures.
An approach that explains differences between human cultures on racial grounds.
Before going further, however, we should warn against turning these categories into rigid boxes.

In reality, there are no sealed boundaries between one approach and another. We therefore have no right to place a particular researcher in one “box” or another and then pass a single, absolute judgment on him.
That kind of rigid judgment would itself violate the method we are using.

The habit of treating the development of human thought in a given society as a sequence of individual thinkers, or as a sequence of their ideas, is widespread in modern histories of Arab-Islamic philosophy.
It is especially common in books prepared for teaching the subject in final-year secondary schools or universities.
In this way, such books help reinforce an idealist way of thinking among generations of school and university students.
One example is a book used by philosophy students preparing for the Lebanese secondary-school certificate, titled Great Figures of Arab Philosophy.

The book shows both sides of this tendency. On the one hand, it presents the history of Arab philosophy as the history of its “great figures.” The title itself is enough to show this. On the other hand, it presents that history as a history of the ideas held by those individuals.
We find an example in the following passage:

“The first person who became known for saying that man has free choice and is not compelled was Maʿbad ibn Khālid al-Juhanī. It is said that he took this idea from a Christian in Iraq who had converted to Islam and later returned to Christianity. Maʿbad’s student, close companion, and successor Ghaylān ibn Marwān al-Dimashqī then took it from him. Ghaylān spread and popularized the idea, argued for it, and defended it vigorously. He later added other views of his own on questions that had become widely debated. His ideas then formed a school, and his followers became a sect known as the Qadarites, whose teaching rested on three main views.”

This is how the Qadarite movement appears: one man has an idea; another man receives it from him and adds further ideas of his own; these ideas then form a school; and the Qadarites become “his followers.”

What disappears from view is the fact that the Qadarite movement was a historical movement, one that arose as an almost direct reflection of a social and political struggle within a society ruled by an absolute hereditary monarchy that justified itself in the name of divine decree and destiny.

The authors of the book do not consider this, even though the historical sources themselves do not identify the beginning of the Qadarite movement with anything like the rigid certainty found in the passage just quoted.
Only an idealist way of thinking can accept such an explanation for the origin of intellectual—or any other—historical phenomena.

The Qadarites also appear here in another way: Maʿbad al-Juhanī supposedly received the idea from a Christian, and so on. In other words, the idea appears as something purely religious, passed from one individual to another, from Christianity into Islam, until it became an Islamic religious issue.
We therefore find two approaches overlapping here.
First, intellectual history is treated as a history of personal ideas isolated from the history of the society in which the people holding those ideas lived.
Second, it is treated as the history of religious ideas with no connection to the earthly problems of human beings.
Both approaches come from an idealist and ahistorical method.

The habit of looking at this heritage only from its religious side, cut off from its human and social roots, is also widespread among modern Arab scholars. It is found even among contemporary writers living in the final decades of the twentieth century.
Consider, for example, what they write about the origins of kalām, philosophy, or Sufism.
How, according to them, did these intellectual traditions—which form some of the central parts of our heritage—come into being?
Their answers are almost all the same, or variations on the same theme.

They generally agree that kalām began as debate over religious doctrine. In the days of the Prophet and his Companions, they say, these debates remained within the religious texts and their obvious meanings. Later, the debates went beyond this and became “the defense of religious beliefs through rational arguments” in response to “foreign influences.”

Some writers define these foreign influences as “a continuing campaign of attack against the new religion and its doctrines,” or as “philosophical attacks coming from different religions, different philosophical beliefs, and various Eastern schools that existed in the lands the Muslims conquered.”
On this point, they are largely in agreement.
They differ more when discussing internal influences.

One writer argues that “the whole of Islamic life is nothing more than an interpretation of the Qurʾān: from studying the Qurʾān’s practical laws came jurisprudence; from studying it as a book dealing with metaphysics came kalām; from studying it as a book concerned with the afterlife came asceticism, Sufism, and ethics; from studying it as a book of government came political science; and from studying its language came the linguistic sciences,” and so on.
Others identify the following internal factors:
“The Qurʾān discussed the main sects and religions that existed in the time of the Prophet Muḥammad—peace be upon him—and answered them and refuted their claims.”

“When the Muslims had finished their conquests, settled down, and become prosperous, their minds began to philosophize about religion. Religious disagreements arose, and they began to examine them and try to reconcile their different aspects. This seems to be a general feature of all the religions we know...”
The disputes centered on the caliphate after the Prophet.
The ambiguous Qurʾānic verses and disagreements over how to interpret them.
To explain the rise of kalām in this way—as modern Arab researchers do in almost all its main outlines, however much their wording or details differ—is to take the question outside history.
The one apparent link with history is their reference to the struggle over the caliphate and its role in the rise of Islamic sects, each of which needed theological arguments to support its position.
But its real historical content was very different from what these writers usually describe.

They treat the caliphate mainly as a religious office. The struggle over it therefore becomes a legal or, in modern terms, “constitutional” disagreement: a dispute over which authority Islamic law had designated to choose the caliph after the Prophet.
The disagreement, on this view, is theoretical and legal. Nothing more.

When some of these writers occasionally call it “political,” their idea of politics remains very shallow. It usually goes no further than the personal ambitions of the individuals competing for the caliphate.
Some go even further and remove even this limited idea of politics from the historical struggle.

One contemporary researcher, for example, finds no “clear conflict” even in the struggle that ended with the killing of the third Rightly Guided Caliph, ʿUthmān. Instead, he sees only “a great preparation for a coming intellectual movement in which debate would intensify...

“There was no major disagreement. The third caliph stood by the Qurʾān and followed the practice of the great Prophet. The Messenger of God died pleased with ʿUthmān, and the two great elders died pleased with ʿUthmān. Even this learned guide of the community, its scholar—indeed the man most devoted to truth,” meaning ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, “was also pleased with the third caliph. What, then, was there to disagree about?”
When the “historical” relation between the rise of kalām and the struggle over the caliphate is treated in this way, through such a metaphysical style of thinking, history itself almost disappears.
Aḥmad Amīn is nearly alone in understanding this relationship historically in a way that comes somewhat closer to the reality of the problem.
He argues that the struggle over the caliphate was political, much like struggles between political parties in our own time, even though parties then did not take the same modern organizational form.

“They took on a strongly religious character. Every political party became a religious sect, and those who fought one another politically also fought one another religiously. Instead of the party being given a political name expressing the political principle it supported, it was given a name expressing a religious doctrine: Shīʿa, Khārijites, Murjiʾa...”
The same applies, he says, to familiar theological questions such as whether a Muslim who committed a major sin was an unbeliever or still a believer:
“It seems that the discussion was not purely theological. Its origin lay in the judgments political parties made about one another...”
But Aḥmad Amīn does not take this sound historical insight far enough.
He does not reach the deeper core of the issue: the social content of the political groupings involved in the conflict.

Because of his bourgeois intellectual and ideological method, we have already seen him explain the Muslims’ “philosophizing about religion” after they had “finished the conquest and settled down” as simply one example of “a general feature of all the religions we know.”
He does not place it within the particular history of that stage of Muslim society—that is, within a political struggle that had a definite social content.

So he retreats from the historical reasoning he had briefly approached when discussing religious-political sects and finally returns the rise of kalām to a purely religious starting point separated from its specific historical conditions.
The bourgeois analyses of the rise of kalām found in these modern studies are not capable of revealing the full dimensions of the problem.
Those dimensions reach back to the social conditions in which Islam first appeared in Mecca. At that time, there was already an embryonic social conflict, though it still took a tribal form.

When the struggle over the caliphate erupted after the Prophet’s death, that earlier conflict now appeared in a religious form. Under the new conditions, it found the forces that allowed it to grow and expand into a social and political struggle far beyond the place and time in which it had first emerged before Islam.
These social and political dimensions did not become fully visible until the caliphate of the third Rightly Guided Caliph, ʿUthmān, and especially in the period immediately after his death.

His killing was connected with the first uprising of its kind in Arab history after Islam, because this uprising openly raised mass demands centered on a clearly defined social and political issue. It had stripped away—or almost stripped away—even its religious form.
This uprising reflected a major development among broad sections of the new society in the newly founded provincial centers.

The killing of Caliph ʿUthmān brought problems that had been developing beneath the surface sharply into the open. They became violent and bloody. Their social and political dimensions appeared with new force, especially after the Umayyad party took hold of them, even though it had itself been one of the direct forces that helped provoke them.
These conflicts inevitably had to find expression in forms of thought that, for historical reasons, took an Islamic religious form.

Out of these intense social problems emerged competing intellectual currents. At first, ideas accumulated unevenly and without any clear system. At the same time, they interacted with several streams of non-Arab culture.
Eventually, this gradual accumulation reached the point where it changed in quality and became a more organized field of knowledge.
Muʿtazilite kalām was this new form.

The same problem appears when modern scholars discuss the Arab-Islamic philosophical heritage. Even contemporary researchers still often use the same approach they use when explaining the origins of kalām.
Philosophy in this heritage is described as “Islamic philosophy.”

For many of these scholars, it is Islamic not in a historical sense—not because it arose within a society whose medieval history was closely tied to Islam and whose political and social system developed under the Islamic caliphate—but in a religious sense: Islamic doctrine and Islamic law.

The historian and philosophical thinker Muṣṭafā ʿAbd al-Rāziq built his analysis of the heritage on this understanding. He used the same meaning when he called the philosophical heritage “Islamic” in the title of his work on its history.

This is why, in his view, Islamic philosophy includes Islamic legal theory, or uṣūl al-fiqh. His reason is that most of the questions discussed in legal theory are, he argues, much like the questions discussed in the study of the foundations of religious doctrine—that is, in kalām.
ʿAbd al-Rāziq does not place Islamic kalām outside “Islamic philosophy.” Instead, he sees the discussions of kalām and legal theory as basic elements in the structure of that philosophy.
For this reason, he even calls al-Shāfiʿī (d. 204 AH/819 CE), the founder of the Sunni legal school named after him, a philosopher.
His reason is that al-Shāfiʿī “developed a method for deriving legal judgments” based on

“the direction of the scientific mind, which is not concerned merely with individual details and branches. His thinking was the thinking of someone who did not focus on isolated questions and disagreements, but sought to organize detailed arguments under general principles that brought them together. That is philosophical reasoning.”
A contemporary Ashʿarite scholar follows a similar path and calls al-Shāfiʿī “Islam’s greatest philosopher of legal principles.”
But this scholar goes further and limits the whole philosophical heritage to the work of Muslim theologians and scholars of legal theory.

The philosophy of al-Kindī, al-Fārābī, Ibn Sīnā, Ibn Rushd, and others “who are called the philosophers of Islam,” he argues, is not “authentic Islamic philosophy.” Instead, it is “Greek in both its general principles and its details, a mixture of Aristotelianism, Platonism, and Neoplatonism.”
Muṣṭafā ʿAbd al-Rāziq does not go that far.

He strongly emphasizes the Islamic character of the philosophical heritage, ties this character to Islamic doctrine and law, and sees this connection as the basis of the originality of “Islamic philosophy.”
Even so, he does not deny the originality of philosophical activity outside theology and legal theory.
He does not take the completely dismissive position adopted by al-Nashshār.
Instead, he places the philosophers and the scholars of theology and legal theory within a single connected intellectual tradition.
